youtube_title: The 'Nobody' Who Built a 100-Year Clan — Except He Was Never a Nobody
youtube_description:
He is remembered as a masterless samurai who rose from nothing. The records tell a different story. Hojo Soun took two provinces without ever being appointed their governor, and his family ruled the Kanto for nearly a century. Even his birth year is still argued: 1432 or 1456, with most scholars now favouring 1456. Follow time-travelling reporter Tokio Kamiya as he files dispatches from Kyoto, Izu, Odawara and the walls of Arai Castle.

📰 Your reporter: Tokio Kamiya, a former Tokyo foreign correspondent. His grandfather's brass pocket watch carries him to one day of Japan's past at a time. He can watch and he can speak, but he can never change what happens. Every episode is his dispatch from the scene.

scenes.narration: I should explain. I am a correspondent, or I was, until my grandfather's brass watch passed to me. It carries me to any moment in Japan's past, for one day at a time. I may watch. I may speak. I may not change a thing. Today it takes me to Kyoto, 1467. Smoke reaches me first. The Onin War has begun, and the shogun, Ashikaga Yoshimasa, cannot stop it. Noble houses empty. Temples burn. Out of this ruin, men with no patience for rank will rise. One of them is about to come into view.

Dramatic documentary scale, ash drifting in the air. No text, no signs, no European elements.

scenes.narration: Now the man himself. The story I grew up with says he was a masterless samurai from Ise, a nobody who arrived with six companions and a dream. I follow the records instead, and they point elsewhere. Most scholars now think he came from a branch of the Ise family, hereditary officials who served the Ashikaga shogun. Not a prince, but hardly a beggar. Even his birth year is argued: 1432 or 1456, with most now favouring the later date. I tell you only what I see. And I see a man who has learned to wait.

scenes.narration: My watch brings me east to Suruga, on the Pacific coast, in 1487. The Imagawa, the ruling house here, has a tie to Soun. Lady Kitagawa, now thought to be his elder sister, married its lord, Yoshitada. In 1476, Yoshitada was killed in battle, and the clan split over who should succeed. Her son Ujichika was a small child. Old accounts say Soun stepped in as a go-between; many scholars doubt it. What is firm is what I see now. The rival claimant is dead, the boy is lord, and Soun holds a castle.

scenes.narration: Next I cross the Hakone ridge into Izu. On paper, this land belongs to the Horigoe Kubo, a branch of the Ashikaga set up to govern eastern Japan. But the household is rotting from within. A quarrel over the succession has turned to blood, and the farmers of Izu are paying for it. I climb a hill above the palace, and I find Soun already there, watching quietly with a few of his men. It is not a great army. He has not come to fight a war. He has come to finish one.

scenes.narration: Around 1493, though historians still argue over the exact year, Soun strikes. I watch him take the Horigoe Palace. Its young master, Chachamaru, has murdered the mother and brother of the new shogun in Kyoto. Now he escapes into the hills, to be hunted down within five years. Soun holds no governor's title here, though Kyoto may quietly approve. There is no heroic charge, only a silent change of master. I put my pencil down. This is what the coming age will be named for.

scenes.narration: At a roadside in Izu, I stop an old farmer. He studies my coat as if I were a travelling merchant, which is what I tell him I am. I ask about the new lord. He tells me the previous household took taxes the way a thief takes coins, and this one at least counts honestly. He has heard that the lord walks the fields himself. He has also heard the lord is not to be trusted. Both, he says, can be true. This is one man's opinion, and I treat it as exactly that.

scenes.narration: Odawara comes next, around 1495 by the common account, though recent research puts it a few years later. The castle belongs to the Omori family, vassals of the powerful Uesugi. The story, and I stress that it is only a story, says Soun asked leave to send beaters into the Hakone hills after stray deer. The beaters were soldiers. By night, the castle was his. I cannot confirm it. What I can confirm is the position. Odawara sits between mountains and sea, on the road to the whole Kanto plain.

scenes.narration: Taking land is one thing. Holding it is another. In the records I read, Soun's rule looks orderly: field surveys, set tax rates, firm control of his retainers. A set of twenty-one articles attributed to him tells his men to rise early, to keep their gear in order, and to be honest. Scholars debate whether he wrote them. But the spirit fits what I see: a man who thinks in years, not days. In a time of plunder, order is a weapon. I note it carefully, in pencil.

scenes.narration: Now he faces the last obstacle, the Miura family, who hold the Miura Peninsula in Sagami. Their castle, Arai, sits on a promontory above the sea, with water on three sides. The siege has dragged on for years. I watch the supply boats thin out. I watch hungry men on the walls. Soun himself, I am told, is somewhere in his sixties or his eighties, and he is still in the field. The wind is cold and salty. Something is about to break.

scenes.narration: 1516. I am on the cliff at Arai when the castle falls. The Miura lord, Yoshiatsu, known as Dosun, fights to the end, and with him his house dies. I listen to the silence after the noise. The defenders are gone. The flags are down. Soun does not cheer. He studies the shoreline as if he were measuring it, and I find I cannot read his face. With the Miura gone, he is master of Sagami as well as Izu, with the Kanto plain open before him. A man who once held a single small castle now holds two provinces.

scenes.narration: 1519. I arrive in Izu, where Soun spends his last days. The records say he dies at Nirayama Castle in the eighth month of that year. I find a quiet room, a lamp, and monks reciting softly. I stay at the edge of the room and ask no questions. My watch ticks in my pocket. Whatever he was, a nobleman's relative or a nobody, he leaves behind two provinces and an heir, Ujitsuna, ready to hold them. The domain he built will outlast him by more than seventy years.

scenes.narration: I jump forward to Odawara, 1523. I watch Ujitsuna, the son, make a quiet but clever choice. He takes the surname Hojo, borrowed from the old regent family of Kamakura. In his father's lifetime, no one called the man Hojo. The change is a claim to legitimacy, a new power wrapping itself in an old and respected name. Historians call this family the Later Hojo, to keep them apart from the earlier regents. I write the new name in my notebook and underline it. They share a name, not a bloodline.

scenes.narration: 1546, Kawagoe. I crouch at the edge of a dark field as Soun's grandson Ujiyasu faces a vast coalition of Uesugi and Ashikaga forces, far larger than his own. By every account, he is outnumbered. At night, he strikes. Torches flare. Men shout in the confusion. By morning, the great army has broken, and I walk the field at dawn. The Hojo, who began with a single small castle, now command much of the Kanto. The family is no longer an upstart. It is a power.

scenes.narration: 1561, Odawara. I climb a hillside as Uesugi Kenshin arrives with a huge army and surrounds the castle. I watch the siege lines tighten around the walls. The defenders do not panic. From up here, they look like men who expect to be believed. The walls hold, the stores last, and after weeks Kenshin withdraws. Takeda Shingen tries his luck in 1569, and he, too, leaves without victory. Odawara becomes a byword for a fortress that cannot be forced. Soun chose this place for its position. His descendants made it a legend.

scenes.narration: Reporter's note. Back in my own century, I think the first thing Soun teaches us is how much Japan loves a rise from nothing. We tell the story of the lone masterless samurai because we want it to be true. The records say he had real connections. I think that makes him more interesting, not less. His talent was to turn connections into something that outlasted favours. Modern Japan still struggles with that balance, between who you know and what you can do.

scenes.narration: Reporter's note. I think Soun's real innovation was the boring kind: surveys, tax rates, rules for retainers. We remember generals. We should also remember the clerks. In my view, modern Japan's quiet faith in procedure, in the well-run office and the punctual timetable, has long roots, and some of them run through men like him. What I saw is only partly documented. What I conclude is my own opinion. A state that keeps its small promises earns the right to ask for big ones.

scenes.narration: Reporter's note. Odawara still remembers the Hojo. Every spring, the city holds a festival with a parade of costumed warriors in their honour. The castle keep you can visit today is a twentieth-century rebuild. I think that is a very Japanese way to hold memory: rebuild, retell, and pass the story to the next generation. But I would add one caution. Stories grow. The tale of the nobody seemed too good to question, until historians checked it.

scenes.narration: Hojo Soun did not invent the age of warring states, but he showed what it rewarded: patience, planning, and the nerve to act when the old order stopped answering. His origins are still argued over, and perhaps always will be. A page in my grandfather's notebook, in my own handwriting, reads only 1868. If you would like the next dispatch to find you, you know where to leave your address. The watch is ticking. Until the next report.
